title: Database Sharding vs Partitioning ⚡ SQL vs NoSQL
ig_caption:
Database Sharding explained: partitioning vs sharding at billion-record scale—how SQL vs NoSQL keeps systems fast?
VIZ 09: same data, two ways to store it (and why joins/migrations feel different).

• SQL: strict relational tables → schema + joins, but careful migration planning
• NoSQL: flexible nested docs → fewer joins, fast reads, evolving structures
• Scaling: horizontal vs vertical scaling
• Under the hood: replication + routing + workload-aware partitioning
• Interview lens: “how do you avoid hotspots and keep queries predictable?”

Practical takeaway: For system design interviews, describe the data model first (entities + access patterns), then choose SQL/NoSQL plus sharding/partition strategy.

Do you prefer SQL consistency with joins, or NoSQL flexibility with nested reads—what would you pick for a billion-record system?

fb_caption:
SQL vs NoSQL is often framed as “schema vs flexibility,” but at scale the real differentiator is how your storage model interacts with partitioning/sharding, query patterns, and operational risk.

In high-scale systems you’ll typically combine:
- Horizontal scaling (more nodes) rather than only vertical (bigger machines)
- Partitioning vs sharding:
  • Partitioning: split data to improve manageability/throughput while keeping a logical model
  • Sharding: split ownership/routing across shards to scale write volume and avoid bottlenecks
- Replication + routing:
  • replicas for read throughput and failover
  • query routing/shard key selection to prevent hotspots

Trade-offs to remember:
1) SQL (relational)
- Pros: clear constraints, strong consistency options, efficient joins when the model fits
- Cons: schema changes and migrations can be costly; cross-shard joins can get expensive fast

2) NoSQL (document/key-value/column families)
- Pros: flexible/nested data, often fewer joins for read-heavy workloads
- Cons: denormalization increases write complexity; enforcing invariants may move to the app layer

Architecture patterns that work in production:
- Start from access patterns (reads/writes, hot keys, query shapes), then pick SQL/NoSQL
- If you need joins across partitions, consider: data modeling changes, precomputed views, or event-driven denormalization
- Design migrations as a first-class system: dual-write/expand-contract strategies (where applicable)
